# Innovation Architecture Rules

<!-- Generated by packages/rules/generate.mjs from data/laws/*.json. Do not edit by hand. -->

The tactics come from public product-discovery and experimentation practice: customer interviews, assumption mapping, smoke tests, service prototypes, pre-commitments, and the innovation-accounting metrics that decide whether any of them was worth running. Each card states a hypothesis with the threshold it pre-commits to, the method (time, cost, confidence), the three stages that run it, and the named false positive that makes that particular test lie.
The hypothesis prints on the card exactly as the source states it, threshold included, because an experiment without its validation criterion is an opinion. The three stages print compressed to one line each; the full stages, the full warning and the method values follow here, because this file is the reference.

## Customer Discovery and Problem Validation Tactics

### I01 — The Mom Test Conversational Protocol

**Hypothesis and threshold.** We believe that [target customer segment] experiences severe operational inefficiency when [executing specific task]. We will verify this by conducting 12 conversational interviews focusing exclusively on past actions, and consider it validated if at least 8 of 12 respondents independently describe a dedicated, imperfect workaround they used within the last 14 days without prompting.

**Schematic.** Moderate confidence: rung 3 of 5

**Method.** Time: 5–7 days · Cost: $0 · Confidence: Moderate (Qualitative behavioral)

**Plan.**
- Preparation: Write five prompts about past events; strip every reference to a solution, a business or a hypothetical.
- Execution: Run 30-minute interviews anchored in the last time they did the task, what it cost, and what they tried first.
- Data collection: Transcribe verbatim; label each line historical behaviour, speculation or feeling, and drop speculation.

**False positive.** Courtesy Bias

Show your concept and interviewees politely affirm it to avoid friction, manufacturing validation.

**Plan as written.**
- Preparation: Formulate 5 open-ended inquiry prompts anchored strictly in historical occurrences. Strip all references to prospective solutions, business concepts, and hypothetical feature sets.
- Execution: Conduct 30-minute semi-structured interviews. Anchor discussions in past events using prompts such as: "Walk me through the last time you completed [task]," "How much time or budget did resolving that bottleneck consume?" and "What alternative approaches failed?".
- Data collection: Record the dialogue verbatim. Classify every statement into three categories: historical behavior, stated forward-looking speculation, or emotional frustration. Disregard speculative statements entirely during synthesis.

**Warning as written.** When interviewers disclose their product concept, interviewees offer polite affirmations to avoid interpersonal friction, generating an illusion of validation.

**Source.** Rob Fitzpatrick (2013). *The Mom Test*. Robfitz.

### I02 — Blank Customer Problem Discovery Interview

**Hypothesis and threshold.** We believe that [industry persona] suffers from [critical operational bottleneck]. We will verify this by executing 15 structured problem interviews across 3 distinct sub-verticals, and consider it validated if ≥ 70% of interviewees rank this problem as one of their top two operational challenges for the current fiscal quarter.

**Schematic.** Moderate confidence: rung 3 of 5

**Method.** Time: 7–10 days · Cost: $0–$100 · Confidence: Moderate

**Plan.**
- Preparation: Define the ideal customer profile from firmographic traits; frame outreach as research, not a sales pitch.
- Execution: Ask for the quarter’s top three operational priorities and see whether the problem surfaces unprompted.
- Data collection: Score urgency one to five from documented budget, executive visibility and active software evaluations.

**False positive.** Polite Problem Inflation

Interviewees lament minor inconveniences they have no budget or mandate to resolve.

**Plan as written.**
- Preparation: Define the Ideal Customer Profile (ICP) based on observable firmographic attributes. Secure interview access by framing outreach as academic or industrial research rather than commercial solicitation.
- Execution: Introduce the macro domain and instruct respondents to identify their top 3 operational priorities for the quarter. Observe whether the hypothesized problem surfaces organically without prompting.
- Data collection: Score the problem's organizational urgency on a 1–5 scale based on documented resource allocation, executive visibility, and active software evaluations.

**Warning as written.** In professional contexts, interviewees frequently lament minor operational inconveniences that they have no budget or mandate to resolve.

**Source.** The source names no originator.

### I03 — Jobs-to-Be-Done (JTBD) Switch and Forces Interview

**Hypothesis and threshold.** We believe that [persona] switches away from [incumbent solution] primarily due to [catalyzing push/pull force]. We will verify this by interviewing 10 individuals who transitioned between solutions within the last 90 days, and consider it validated if ≥ 60% point to the exact same triggering event and emotional crisis point.

**Schematic.** Moderate-High confidence: rung 4 of 5

**Method.** Time: 7–14 days · Cost: $0–$250 · Confidence: Moderate-High

**Plan.**
- Preparation: Recruit ten people who switched in the last 90 days and build the four-force inquiry matrix.
- Execution: Walk the arc - first thought, active looking, deciding, consuming - and ask what nearly stopped the purchase.
- Data collection: Map the active forces on a matrix, keeping push mechanisms apart from feature wishlists.

**False positive.** Post-Hoc Rationalization

Buyers build coherent narratives for decisions that were emotional, impulsive or organisational.

**Plan as written.**
- Preparation: Recruit participants who recently switched products within the category. Construct an inquiry matrix covering the four core forces: Push of the Current Situation, Pull of the New Solution, Habit/Inertia, and Anxiety of Change.
- Execution: Interrogate the chronological arc of the transition: First Thought, Active Looking, Deciding, and Consuming. Inquire: "Where were you when you decided the prior solution was untenable?" "What almost prevented you from finalizing the purchase?"
- Data collection: Map the active forces onto a Cartesian matrix, separating push mechanisms from unvalidated feature wishlists.

**Warning as written.** Consumers routinely construct coherent, rational narratives for purchasing decisions that were fundamentally driven by emotional, impulsive, or organizational impulses.

**Source.** Clayton M. Christensen, Taddy Hall, Karen Dillon & David S. Duncan (2016). *Competing Against Luck: The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice*. HarperBusiness.

### I04 — Ethnographic Contextual Inquiry (Shadowing)

**Hypothesis and threshold.** We believe that [operators] face unrecorded cognitive overload while [operating system X]. We will verify this by observing 6 operators in their natural workplace for 4 hours each, and consider it validated if we record ≥ 5 unprompted compensatory mechanisms (e.g., sticky notes, personal spreadsheets, ad-hoc scripts) per operator per shift.

**Schematic.** High confidence: rung 5 of 5

**Method.** Time: 10–14 days · Cost: $0–$500 · Confidence: High (Direct observation)

**Plan.**
- Preparation: Clear confidentiality and access; build a ledger for micro-interruptions, non-verbal cues and app switches.
- Execution: Observe silently through a shift; interrupt only on a deviation and ask what motivated that step.
- Data collection: Compile a minute-by-minute trace of application switches, error recovery, movement and distraction.

**False positive.** Hawthorne Effect

Observed operators tidy their workarounds and follow formal protocol because someone is watching.

**Plan as written.**
- Preparation: Execute confidentiality agreements and workplace access protocols. Construct an observation ledger focused on micro-interruptions, non-verbal cues, and application-switching frequency.
- Execution: Observe the operator silently during regular shifts. Interrupt only when an operational deviation occurs: "I observed you copied that string into an external editor before pasting it. What motivated that step?"
- Data collection: Compile a minute-by-minute workflow trace logging application switches, error recovery efforts, physical movements, and environmental distractions.

**Warning as written.** Subjects alter their conventional workflows, adhere more strictly to formal protocols, or tidy operational workarounds simply because they are being observed.

**Source.** Hugh Beyer & Karen Holtzblatt (1998). *Contextual Design: Defining Customer-Centered Systems*. Morgan Kaufmann.

### I05 — Value Proposition Canvas Customer Profiling

**Hypothesis and threshold.** We believe that [customer segment] considers [pain point Y] significantly more critical than [pain point Z]. We will verify this by conducting 10 canvas alignment exercises, and consider it validated if ≥ 75% of participants independently cluster their top 3 jobs and pains into identical operational nodes.

**Schematic.** Moderate confidence: rung 3 of 5

**Method.** Time: 3–5 days · Cost: $0 · Confidence: Moderate

**Plan.**
- Preparation: Lay out an empty customer profile of jobs, pains and gains on a board that participants can move.
- Execution: Run an unmoderated card sort into functional, social and emotional categories, then rank pains and gains.
- Data collection: Record where items cluster and correlate the rankings across participants.

**False positive.** Aspirational Self-Deception

People elevate noble social and emotional jobs above the mundane functional tasks that decide the purchase.

**Plan as written.**
- Preparation: Construct an unpopulated Value Proposition Canvas Customer Profile (comprising Jobs, Pains, and Gains) using standardized markdown or digital boards.
- Execution: Guide users through an unmoderated card-sort protocol. Instruct them to place operational responsibilities into functional, social, and emotional categories, then rank pains by severity and gains by relevance.
- Data collection: Record the spatial clustering of items. Calculate Spearman rank-order correlation coefficients across participant cards.

**Warning as written.** Participants consistently overemphasize noble emotional or social jobs while minimizing the mundane, repetitive functional tasks that dictate enterprise purchase behavior.

**Source.** Alexander Osterwalder, Yves Pigneur, Gregory Bernarda & Alan Smith (2014). *Value Proposition Design: How to Create Products and Services Customers Want*. John Wiley & Sons.

### I06 — Customer Churn and Exit Interview Mining

**Hypothesis and threshold.** We believe that customers abandon [incumbent solution category] because of [deficiency X]. We will verify this by auditing 20 canceled customer accounts or exit interviews, and consider it validated if ≥ 50% identify [deficiency X] as their primary non-negotiable exit driver rather than pricing or budget constraints.

**Schematic.** High confidence: rung 5 of 5

**Method.** Time: 7–12 days · Cost: $0 · Confidence: High (Post-behavioral)

**Plan.**
- Preparation: Pull accounts cancelled in the last 30 to 60 days; frame the call as a process post-mortem, not a win-back.
- Execution: Ask when value stopped, what workaround they built before leaving, and what replaced the product.
- Data collection: Code each exit into price, product defect, reorganisation or loss of internal champion.

**False positive.** Scapegoat Rationalization

Churned clients blame price or a peripheral bug rather than admit the organisation could not adopt it.

**Plan as written.**
- Preparation: Extract lists of accounts canceled within the prior 30–60 days. Frame interview outreach as an operational post-mortem aimed at process improvement rather than customer win-back.
- Execution: Conduct 20-minute structured exit interviews inquiring: "At what specific moment did the product cease delivering anticipated value?" "What workaround did you build prior to cancellation?" "What replacement system was deployed?"
- Data collection: Code exit rationales into root categories: price sensitivity, core product defect, organizational reorganization, or loss of internal champion.

**Warning as written.** Churned clients routinely point to price or peripheral software bugs as polite covers rather than acknowledging their organization lacked the operational competence to adopt the platform.

**Source.** The source names no originator.

### I07 — Public Community and Social Sentiment Mining

**Hypothesis and threshold.** We believe that users of [incumbent software] are actively seeking alternatives due to [specific systemic flaw]. We will verify this by analyzing 300 unresolved negative comments and support threads across industry forums, and consider it validated if ≥ 25% of organic complaint threads focus specifically on [flaw].

**Schematic.** Low-Moderate confidence: rung 2 of 5

**Method.** Time: 3–5 days · Cost: $0 · Confidence: Low-Moderate

**Plan.**
- Preparation: Map the practitioner communities: specialist forums, issue trackers, subreddits and professional groups.
- Execution: Search with diagnostic boolean strings - how do I fix, alternative to, terrible UX, workaround.
- Data collection: Group complaints into themes, reported losses and the operational driver under each.

**False positive.** Selection Bias of Vocal Minorities

Public threads amplify edge-case power users whose needs diverge from the mainstream market.

**Plan as written.**
- Preparation: Map primary practitioner communities across specialized forums, GitHub issue trackers, subreddit channels, and professional discussion spaces.
- Execution: Execute systematic diagnostic search queries using boolean strings (e.g., "how do I fix", "alternative to", "terrible UX", "workaround").
- Data collection: Aggregate complaint structures into an analysis matrix. Track recurring themes, estimated financial losses reported by users, and underlying operational drivers.

**Warning as written.** Public communities amplify the grievances of highly vocal edge-case power users whose requirements diverge significantly from the mainstream market.

**Source.** The source names no originator.

### I08 — Customer Advisory Board Problem Council

**Hypothesis and threshold.** We believe that [industry vertical] executives consider [nascent regulatory or operational challenge] a board-level risk. We will verify this by hosting a 6-executive roundtable, and consider it validated if ≥ 4 members confirm they have formally committed budget to mitigate the issue in the current fiscal year.

**Schematic.** Moderate confidence: rung 3 of 5

**Method.** Time: 14–21 days · Cost: $500–$$$ · Confidence: Moderate

**Plan.**
- Preparation: Recruit six non-competing executives and frame the session as an off-the-record working council.
- Execution: Under the Chatham House Rule, have each name their single greatest vulnerability, with no product pitch.
- Data collection: Record how peers validate each other, which budget lines are disclosed, and which problems recur.

**False positive.** Executive Echo Chamber

Executives echo industry buzzwords to look forward-thinking before peers, regardless of budget.

**Plan as written.**
- Preparation: Recruit 6 non-competing industry executives. Frame the session as an off-the-record working council on emerging operational bottlenecks.
- Execution: Facilitate an executive Chatham House Rule discussion around operational risks. Require each participant to detail their single greatest vulnerability without evaluating potential software solutions.
- Data collection: Record the level of inter-participant validation, specific budget line items disclosed, and shared operational challenges that surface organically across accounts.

**Warning as written.** Board members often echo high-level industry buzzwords and macro narratives to appear forward-thinking before peers, irrespective of actual internal budget allocation.

**Source.** The source names no originator.

### I09 — Search Intent and Semantic Volume Reconnaissance

**Hypothesis and threshold.** We believe that consumers are actively searching for ways to solve [problem X]. We will verify this by analyzing search engine queries across targeted keyword groups, and consider it validated if high-intent terms show ≥ 2,500 monthly organic queries with a year-over-year growth rate of ≥ 20%.

**Schematic.** Moderate confidence: rung 3 of 5

**Method.** Time: 2–4 days · Cost: $0–$150 · Confidence: Moderate (Intent-based)

**Plan.**
- Preparation: Compile seed variants of high-intent syntax: how to automate X, X alternative, X compliance template.
- Execution: Query volume databases for regional density, historical trend, cost per click and competitor saturation.
- Data collection: Split queries into informational, navigational, commercial and transactional, then total commercial volume.

**False positive.** Informational Intent Conflation

High informational volume can mean curiosity or free-guide seekers, not buyers with commercial intent.

**Plan as written.**
- Preparation: Compile a seed dictionary of high-intent search syntax variants (e.g., "how to automate X", "X alternative", "X compliance template").
- Execution: Query search volume databases to extract regional search density, historical trajectory, cost-per-click bids, and competitor domain saturation.
- Data collection: Segment search queries into Informational, Navigational, Commercial, and Transactional categories. Calculate the total addressable commercial search volume.

**Warning as written.** High search volumes for informational queries often signify academic curiosity or individuals looking for free guides, rather than buyers demonstrating commercial intent.

**Source.** The source names no originator.

### I10 — Critical Incident Technique (CIT) Audit

**Hypothesis and threshold.** We believe that [event X] triggers operational failure in [workflow Y]. We will verify this by collecting 15 detailed critical incident reports from practitioners, and consider it validated if ≥ 80% report that the incident caused acute workflow delays, compliance exposure, or direct financial loss.

**Schematic.** High confidence: rung 5 of 5

**Method.** Time: 5–8 days · Cost: $0 · Confidence: High (Incident-focused)

**Plan.**
- Preparation: Set explicit inclusion criteria for a critical incident: downtime, SLA breach or emergency briefing.
- Execution: Ask practitioners to recount the most recent failure, the conditions before it, and what failed in response.
- Data collection: Build a chronological event map per incident: root trigger, compounding effects, downstream cost.

**False positive.** Salience and Availability Bias

Vivid crises are remembered clearly and mistaken for routine, recurring market needs.

**Plan as written.**
- Preparation: Establish explicit inclusion criteria for what constitutes a critical incident (e.g., unscheduled downtime, SLA breach, or emergency executive briefing).
- Execution: Interview qualified practitioners using the CIT protocol: "Recount the most recent operational failure in your workflow. What specific conditions preceded it? What interventions were deployed, and what systems failed?"
- Data collection: Reconstruct a chronological event map for each incident, detailing the root triggers, secondary compounding effects, and downstream financial costs.

**Warning as written.** Participants recall dramatic, emotionally charged anomalies with extreme clarity, leading researchers to mistake infrequent operational crises for routine, recurring market needs.

**Source.** John C. Flanagan (1954). *The Critical Incident Technique*. Psychological Bulletin.

## Hypothesis Framing and Assumption Mapping Tactics

### I11 — Desirability, Feasibility, and Viability (DFV) Mapping

**Hypothesis and threshold.** We believe that our cross-functional team holds strategic alignment on our core business vulnerabilities. We will verify this by mapping all operational assumptions across a 2 × 2 matrix (Impact vs. Evidence), and consider it validated if participants achieve ≥ 90% consensus on the top 5 assumptions categorized in the High Impact / Low Evidence quadrant.

**Schematic.** Low confidence: rung 1 of 5

**Method.** Time: 1–2 days · Cost: $0 · Confidence: Low (Conceptual alignment)

**Plan.**
- Preparation: Assemble product, engineering, design and commercial leads with desirability, feasibility, viability cards.
- Execution: Have each write their explicit premises, then place every assumption on a shared impact-by-evidence grid.
- Data collection: Cluster overlapping cards into themes and isolate high-impact, low-evidence as the experiment backlog.

**False positive.** HiPPO Distortion

Senior executives drag risky assumptions into the known quadrant on personal conviction.

**Plan as written.**
- Preparation: Assemble product, engineering, design, and commercial leaders. Provide each member with assumption tracking cards categorized into Desirability, Feasibility, and Viability.
- Execution: Instruct members to independently document explicit operational premises. Place every assumption onto a shared 2 × 2 grid: Vertical Axis = Impact (Low vs. High); Horizontal Axis = Current Evidence (Known vs. Unknown).
- Data collection: Cluster overlapping cards into distinct operational themes. Isolate the High Impact / Low Evidence quadrant as the designated experiment backlog.

**Warning as written.** Senior executives frequently drag high-risk assumptions into the "Known" quadrant based entirely on personal conviction, blinding the team to critical structural vulnerabilities.

**Source.** The source names no originator.

### I12 — Riskiest Assumption Test (RAT) Decomposition

**Hypothesis and threshold.** We believe that [Assumption A] represents the single existential bottleneck for the business model. We will verify this by decomposing the business concept into causal dependency trees, and consider it validated if breaking this single assumption mathematically invalidates all downstream unit economics.

**Schematic.** Moderate confidence: rung 3 of 5

**Method.** Time: 2–3 days · Cost: $0 · Confidence: Moderate

**Plan.**
- Preparation: Take the top-ranked assumption from the DFV matrix and break it into discrete component premises.
- Execution: Build a causal tree of what must be true and trace back to the premise whose failure collapses it.
- Data collection: Write the test specification for that root: thresholds, time boundaries and required evidence weight.

**False positive.** Premature Optimization of Secondary Assumptions

Teams test easy details - interface polish, onboarding copy - while skipping the existential risk.

**Plan as written.**
- Preparation: Isolate the top-ranked assumption from the DFV matrix. Break it down into discrete component premises.
- Execution: Construct a causal dependency tree using "What Must Be True" statements. Trace dependencies backward to identify the foundational premise whose failure collapses the entire structure.
- Data collection: Draft a dedicated testing specification for this root assumption, detailing validation thresholds, temporal boundaries, and required evidence weights.

**Warning as written.** Teams frequently expend energy testing easily measurable operational details (such as interface aesthetics or onboarding micro-copy) while sidestepping existential commercial viability risks.

**Source.** The source names no originator.

### I13 — Problem-Solution Fit Scorecarding

**Hypothesis and threshold.** We believe our proposed solution addresses the primary pain points discovered in Phase 1. We will verify this by scoring our feature set against validated customer problems using a blind scoring rubric, and consider it validated if ≥ 80% of features map directly to high-severity problems, with all secondary unmapped features eliminated.

**Schematic.** Moderate confidence: rung 3 of 5

**Method.** Time: 3–5 days · Cost: $0 · Confidence: Moderate

**Plan.**
- Preparation: List validated customer problems on the vertical axis and proposed feature specifications across the top.
- Execution: For each intersection ask whether the feature relieves that problem, and justify it with phase-one data.
- Data collection: Compute the coverage ratio; drop features that solve unvalidated problems or miss the core bottleneck.

**False positive.** Sunk Cost Feature Attachment

Teams write elaborate post-hoc justifications for favourite features with no link to validated problems.

**Plan as written.**
- Preparation: Construct a matrix listing validated customer problems on the vertical axis and proposed feature specifications on the horizontal axis.
- Execution: Evaluate each intersection: Does this feature directly alleviate this specific problem? Require cross-functional leads to justify each connection with behavioral data gathered in Phase 1.
- Data collection: Calculate the operational coverage ratio. Flag and discard features that solve unvalidated problems or fail to resolve the core bottleneck.

**Warning as written.** Product teams routinely construct elaborate post-hoc justifications for favorite features that have no demonstrable link to validated customer problems.

**Source.** The source names no originator.

### I14 — Stakeholder and Buying Center Influence Mapping (B2B)

**Hypothesis and threshold.** We believe that [Role A] controls purchase authority, while [Role B] serves as an internal champion. We will verify this by mapping the buying center dynamics across 8 enterprise target accounts, and consider it validated if the operational economic buyer matches our target persona in ≥ 75% of evaluated org charts.

**Schematic.** Moderate-High confidence: rung 4 of 5

**Method.** Time: 5–7 days · Cost: $0 · Confidence: Moderate-High

**Plan.**
- Preparation: Define the six buying roles: economic buyer, champion, end user, technical gatekeeper, procurement, blocker.
- Execution: Call across departments in each account and ask whose budget pays and who holds the veto in review.
- Data collection: Chart the decision, veto and capital-authorisation path for each of the eight accounts.

**False positive.** Champion Conflation

An enthusiastic end user is mistaken for the economic buyer, and the deal stalls at procurement.

**Plan as written.**
- Preparation: Define the six canonical enterprise purchasing roles: Economic Buyer, Champion, End User, Technical Gatekeeper, Procurement, and Blocker.
- Execution: Conduct organizational discovery calls across multiple departments within each target account. Ask: "Whose departmental budget pays for this solution?" "Who possesses absolute veto authority during procurement and security review?".
- Data collection: Chart the formal decision, veto, and capital authorization pathways for each enterprise account.

**Warning as written.** Founders routinely mistake an enthusiastic end-user champion for the economic buyer, discovering too late that the deal stalls indefinitely when presented to procurement.

**Source.** The source names no originator.

### I15 — Value Proposition Fit Matrix (Relievers vs. Pains)

**Hypothesis and threshold.** We believe that our core value proposition outranks existing market alternatives on speed and clarity. We will verify this by presenting a relative comparison matrix to 12 prospective users, and consider it validated if ≥ 70% prioritize our specific pain relievers over incumbent alternatives.

**Schematic.** Moderate confidence: rung 3 of 5

**Method.** Time: 2–4 days · Cost: $0 · Confidence: Moderate

**Plan.**
- Preparation: Build a two-sided canvas that maps pain relievers to customer pains and gain creators to gains.
- Execution: Have target users rate each element’s clarity, relevance and difference against their current alternative.
- Data collection: Score fit with a weighted model calibrated to the pains users ranked highest.

**False positive.** Theoretical Value Congruence

A proposition can read as cohesive and compelling on paper and still not move anyone off the incumbent.

**Plan as written.**
- Preparation: Build a two-sided Value Proposition Canvas explicitly mapping Pain Relievers to Customer Pains and Gain Creators to Customer Gains.
- Execution: Conduct structured review sessions where target users evaluate the clarity, relevance, and differentiation of each value proposition element against their current operational alternatives.
- Data collection: Quantify the fit score using a weighted distribution model calibrated to user-prioritized pain points.

**Warning as written.** A value proposition can appear conceptually cohesive and compelling on paper while failing to generate sufficient switching momentum to overcome incumbent inertia.

**Source.** Alexander Osterwalder, Yves Pigneur, Gregory Bernarda & Alan Smith (2014). *Value Proposition Design: How to Create Products and Services Customers Want*. John Wiley & Sons.

### I16 — Reverse-Income Economic Viability Model

**Hypothesis and threshold.** We believe this business model can achieve sustainable profitability at target scale. We will verify this by building a reverse unit-economics model, and consider it validated if the required conversion rates and average revenue per user (ARPU) remain within historical benchmark ranges for this industry vertical.

**Schematic.** High confidence: rung 5 of 5

**Method.** Time: 1–2 days · Cost: $0 · Confidence: High (Mathematical proof)

**Plan.**
- Preparation: Fix an ambitious revenue milestone, such as ten million in annual recurring revenue.
- Execution: Work backward from revenue: required customers = ARR / ARPU, then conversion and acquisition cost.
- Data collection: Check the required metrics against benchmarks: Required Leads = Target ARR / (ARPU × Funnel Conversion Rate).

**False positive.** Spreadsheet Viability Syndrome

A model balances by inserting aggressive growth or fantasy acquisition costs, hiding an unviable business.

**Plan as written.**
- Preparation: Fix an ambitious financial milestone (e.g., 10,000,000 ARR).
- Execution: Work backward to calculate the necessary funnel metrics: divide target revenue by expected ARPU to determine the required customer volume, then calculate the necessary conversion rates and acquisition costs across the funnel.
- Data collection: Compare required operational metrics against real-world industry benchmarks: Required Leads = Target ARR / (ARPU × Funnel Conversion Rate)

**Warning as written.** Financial models can always be balanced by inserting aggressive compound growth rates or unrealistically low customer acquisition costs, masking unviable business fundamentals.

**Source.** The source names no originator.

### I17 — Technical Feasibility Spike and Architecture Proof

**Hypothesis and threshold.** We believe that [external API / architecture] can process [X volume] within [Y latency]. We will verify this by deploying an isolated technical spike in a staging environment, and consider it validated if latency remains below 250ms at 1,500 concurrent requests without data loss.

**Schematic.** High confidence: rung 5 of 5

**Method.** Time: 3–7 days · Cost: $0–$$$ · Confidence: High (Empirical technical)

**Plan.**
- Preparation: Strip the front end and every non-essential dependency; isolate the one algorithmic or throughput unknown.
- Execution: Build the smallest codebase that can stress the integration, algorithm or pipeline at the target load.
- Data collection: Run automated load scripts and log latency distribution, memory, error codes and compute cost.

**False positive.** Sandbox Isolation Bias

A clean staging spike degrades on real edge cases, dirty legacy data and unoptimised production dependencies.

**Plan as written.**
- Preparation: Strip away all frontend interfaces and non-essential dependencies. Isolate the specific algorithmic or data throughput unknown.
- Execution: Build a minimal codebase designed solely to stress-test the core integration, algorithm, or data pipeline.
- Data collection: Run automated load scripts, logging latency distributions, memory usage, error codes, and compute costs.

**Warning as written.** A technical architecture that operates smoothly in a clean, isolated staging environment often degrades when exposed to real-world edge cases, dirty legacy data, and unoptimized production dependencies.

**Source.** The source names no originator.

### I18 — Regulatory and Compliance Gate Audit

**Hypothesis and threshold.** We believe our proposed data architecture complies fully with relevant regulatory standards (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, SOC2). We will verify this by completing a formal compliance audit with an external specialist, and consider it validated if the audit reveals zero critical regulatory blockers that would require fundamentally altering the product model.

**Schematic.** High confidence: rung 5 of 5

**Method.** Time: 5–10 days · Cost: $0–$$$$ · Confidence: High

**Plan.**
- Preparation: Document data lifecycles, consent mechanisms, storage tiers and cross-border transfer paths.
- Execution: Walk legal and compliance specialists through the end-to-end data flow to find every regulatory touchpoint.
- Data collection: Log legal hurdles, certification costs and implementation timelines against the product model.

**False positive.** Informal Legal Assurances

Casual early guidance from corporate counsel is mistaken for formal, binding regulatory clearance.

**Plan as written.**
- Preparation: Document data lifecycles, user consent mechanisms, storage tiers, and cross-border transfer paths.
- Execution: Walk legal and compliance specialists through the end-to-end data flow to identify regulatory touchpoints.
- Data collection: Log potential legal hurdles, compliance requirements, certification expenses, and expected implementation timelines.

**Warning as written.** Early-stage teams frequently mistake casual, preliminary guidance from corporate attorneys for formal, binding regulatory clearance.

**Source.** The source names no originator.

### I19 — Acquisition Channel Scalability Matrix

**Hypothesis and threshold.** We believe that [Channel X] can sustainably deliver customer acquisition at targeted unit costs. We will verify this by cross-referencing industry channel benchmarks against product characteristics, and consider it validated if the channel delivers an estimated CAC:LTV ratio of ≥ 1:3 at target market scale.

**Schematic.** Moderate confidence: rung 3 of 5

**Method.** Time: 3–5 days · Cost: $0 · Confidence: Moderate

**Plan.**
- Preparation: Map candidate acquisition channels against ARPU tiers and the way the target users actually buy.
- Execution: Drop channels that cannot carry the price point - enterprise direct sales rarely pays below $1,000 ARPU.
- Data collection: Build a projection matrix of saturation, cost-per-click trend and conversion assumptions per channel.

**False positive.** Channel Mirage Effect

Traction in niche or closed communities rarely scales when broad advertising is switched on.

**Plan as written.**
- Preparation: Map potential acquisition channels against ARPU tiers and user buying habits.
- Execution: Eliminate channels that don't match the product's price point (e.g., enterprise direct sales forces are rarely viable for products with an ARPU under $1,000/year).
- Data collection: Build a channel projection matrix comparing expected saturation points, cost-per-click trends, and estimated conversion rates.

**Warning as written.** Early customer acquisition traction achieved in niche communities or closed groups rarely scales efficiently once broader advertising channels are deployed.

**Source.** The source names no originator.

### I20 — Van Westendorp Price Sensitivity Meter

**Hypothesis and threshold.** We believe that the acceptable price band for our offering falls between [Price A] and [Price B]. We will verify this by surveying 50 qualified target customers using the four standard Van Westendorp questions, and consider it validated if the Indifference Price Point aligns with our planned market pricing within a ±10% margin.

**Schematic.** Moderate-High confidence: rung 4 of 5

**Method.** Time: 5–7 days · Cost: $50–$300 · Confidence: Moderate-High

**Plan.**
- Preparation: Build the survey around the four price questions: too cheap, a bargain, getting expensive, too expensive.
- Execution: Send the instrument only to qualified buyers who match the defined ideal customer profile.
- Data collection: Plot the cumulative curves; read the indifference and optimal price points and compare with the plan price.

**False positive.** Stated Willingness Bias

Stated-price surveys overestimate what people pay when asked to enter real payment details.

**Plan as written.**
- Preparation: Construct a survey detailing the core value proposition. Include the four standard pricing questions: (1) At what price is it too cheap to trust the quality? (2) A bargain? (3) Getting expensive, but still worth considering? (4) Too expensive to consider?
- Execution: Distribute the instrument strictly to qualified target buyers who match the defined ICP.
- Data collection: Plot cumulative distribution curves to identify the Indifference Price Point (intersection of "Cheap" and "Expensive") and the Optimal Price Point (intersection of "Too Cheap" and "Too Expensive"): Optimal Price Point (OPP) = Intersection of "Too Cheap" and "Too Expensive"

**Warning as written.** Theoretical pricing surveys reliably overestimate how much customers will actually spend when asked to enter real payment details.

**Source.** Peter H. Van Westendorp (1976). *NSS-Price Sensitivity Meter (PSM): A New Approach to Study Consumer Perception of Price*. Proceedings of the 29th ESOMAR Congress.

## Low-Fidelity Prototyping and Smoke Testing Tactics

### I30 — Refundable Deposit Pre-Order

**Hypothesis and threshold.** We believe users will pay [Price Y] for our forthcoming product. We will verify this by running a pre-order campaign with a required, refundable $50 reservation deposit, and consider it validated if ≥ 3.0% of unique page visitors complete the checkout transaction.

**Schematic.** Payment at step 2 of the 3-step strip

**Method.** Time: 7–14 days · Cost: $100–$500 · Confidence: Extreme (Financial commitment)

**Plan.**
- Preparation: State the product is in development and offer priority queue placement for a refundable deposit.
- Execution: Drive qualified traffic to the reservation page and process real payments via a gateway.
- Data collection: Measure payment completion, refunds requested, and checkout questions.

**False positive.** Frictionless Refund Psychology

When deposits are low and refundable, buyers treat checkout as a bookmark rather than a commitment.

**Plan as written.**
- Preparation: Build a checkout flow that clearly states the product is in active development, offering priority queue placement in exchange for a refundable deposit.
- Execution: Drive qualified traffic to the reservation page and process real financial transactions via a payment gateway.
- Data collection: Measure payment completion rates, refund requests, and customer questions submitted during checkout.

**Warning as written.** When deposits are low, fully refundable, and clearly framed as risk-free, conversion rates often artificially inflate, as buyers treat the checkout as an easy way to bookmark the product rather than an actual purchase commitment.

**Source.** The source names no originator.

## Metrics, Telemetry, and Innovation Accounting Tactics

### I37 — Unit Economics Stress Test (CAC:LTV Ratio)

**Hypothesis and threshold.** We believe our customer acquisition model is economically sustainable. We will verify this by measuring blended and paid Customer Acquisition Costs alongside early cohort churn and revenue, and consider it validated if the projected Lifetime Value to Customer Acquisition Cost ratio exceeds 3:1, with full CAC payback achieved in ≤ 12 months: LTV / CAC ≥ 3.0, where LTV = (ARPU × Gross Margin) / Churn Rate

**Schematic.** Read at step 3 of the 3-step strip

**Method.** Time: 30–60 days · Cost: $500–$$$$ · Confidence: High

**Plan.**
- Preparation: Aggregate fully loaded acquisition costs across a 60-day window: spend, commissions, overhead, tools.
- Execution: Track paid customer accounts generated specifically from those spend allocations.
- Data collection: Calculate CAC payback months and the projected LTV to CAC ratio.

**False positive.** Blended CAC Smuggling

Blending organic traffic with paid spend hides high paid acquisition costs and an unviable channel.

**Plan as written.**
- Preparation: Aggregate all fully loaded acquisition costs (ad spend, sales commissions, operational overhead, marketing software) across a 60-day testing window.
- Execution: Track the total number of paid customer accounts generated specifically from those spend allocations.
- Data collection: Calculate the months required to recover customer acquisition costs: Payback Period (Months) = CAC / (ARPU × Gross Margin %)

**Warning as written.** Blending cheap organic, direct, or personal network traffic with paid marketing spend obscures high paid customer acquisition costs, hiding an unviable acquisition channel.

**Source.** The source names no originator.

### I39 — Micro-Conversion Step Drop-Off Audit

**Hypothesis and threshold.** We believe that [Step 3 in our onboarding flow] causes unnecessary user drop-off. We will verify this by instrumenting telemetry across every form field and screen transition, and consider it validated if simplifying that single step reduces drop-off by ≥ 30% without lowering downstream activation quality.

**Schematic.** Read at step 3 of the 3-step strip

**Method.** Time: 7–14 days · Cost: $0 · Confidence: High

**Plan.**
- Preparation: Map every field, click and screen transition in the target path into a sequential funnel.
- Execution: Log drop-off, validation errors and interaction times across 500 sessions.
- Data collection: Plot the drop-off gradient across each micro-step to find friction.

**False positive.** Removing Essential Friction

Cutting identity checks or qualification questions raises completion and floods the product with junk accounts.

**Plan as written.**
- Preparation: Map every user input field, click, and screen transition in the target path into a sequential funnel model.
- Execution: Log drop-off percentages, validation errors, and interaction times for every field across 500 user sessions.
- Data collection: Plot the drop-off gradient across each micro-step to identify points of user friction.

**Warning as written.** Streamlining onboarding forms by cutting out identity checks or qualification questions can boost completion rates while flooding the product with unqualified or spam accounts.

**Source.** The source names no originator.
